### Objective:

This is a tutorial on how to make a basic, publishable plot in R. A basic understanding of R is useful in interpreting the code, but is not required. For more info on base R scripting, visit ["An Introduction to R"](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-intro.html). 

---

### **First thing's first, let's load our libraries.**

Libraries we will use today are:

- *tidyverse*

- *here*

- *rsconnect*

- *palmerpenguins*

- *kableExtra*

Click "**Show code**" below to see a description of each library.

```{r}

library(tidyverse)      # contains ggplot and other essential functions
library(here)           # allows for cleaner saving 
library(rsconnect)      # allows for easy publishing
library(palmerpenguins) # contains the penguin data
library(kableExtra)     # for making neat tables

```

Once the packages are loaded, we can use their functions in scripts.

---

### **Check out the data**

A function is a specific word followed by a parenthesis. 

Click "**Show code**" below to see an example of a simple function we can use to look at the data:

```{r}

#print the first few rows of the penguin data

head(penguins)

```

This isn't great for viewing purposes, the last two columns are cut off! Let's form this into a proper table to view the first five lines of data.

---

### **Basic table**
Just the top five rows to see what's going on. 
Click "**Show code**" to see the detailed breakdown of each line.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-test1
#| tbl-cap: "Data preview table"
#| tbl-align: "center"

# this |> symbol is called a "pipe". Use this to tell R to do something with 
#a dataset. The code following it contains the instructions.
penguins |>
  
  # slice() can be used to select a specific number of rows from a dataset. 
  # In this case, we want the first five rows, and we want to pipe that into
  # the next function:
  slice(0:5) |> 
  
  # kbl() is a function from kableExtra. This creates a neater table.
  kbl() |> 
  
  # This command sets the theme of the table:
  kable_classic() |> 
  
  # and finally, this command identifies the first row "0", and makes the font
  # bold, the color of the text a dark gray, and the background a nice gold.
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = "black", background = "#fed766")

```

Now that we can see what we're working with, let's say we want to look at how bill geometry differs across **penguin species** and **islands**.
To do this, let's begin by making a *basic plot*.

---

### **Basic plot scripting**

Click on "**Show code**" below to see a quick script to make a simple plot. This will give us a very basic view of all the bill length and bill depth data by species.

```{r}
#| label: fig-basic
#| fig-cap: "Basic plot of bill length compared with bill depth. Separated into different colors by species."
#| fig-align: "center"

# First, pipe penguins into the plotting function
penguins |> 
  
  # The ggplot function makes the base plot
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = bill_length_mm,    # sets the x axis
                       y = bill_depth_mm,     # sets the y axis
                       color = species)) +    # colors the data by species
  geom_point()      # this is what actually puts the points on the plot.
```

This is great, but it would be even better if we could see the differences between each island.

---

### **Let's facet wrap that to see the difference between islands**

Click "**Show code**" to see the facet_wrap addition.

```{r}
#| label: fig-basic2
#| fig-cap: "Adding a facet wrap to explore the differences between islands."
#| fig-align: "center"
penguins |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = bill_length_mm,
                       y = bill_depth_mm,
                       color = species)) +
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~island, scales = "free")  # facet_wrap allows us to view by
                                        # island, and the scales = free
                                        # makes each graph have its own scale.
```

Nice! However, in @fig-basic2, the labels are not great. There is no title, and the island names have no context. We can fix them!

---

### **Let's add some better labels**

Click "**Show code**" below to see how labels are added and modified.

```{r}
#| label: fig-basic3
#| fig-cap: "Adding better labels in the form of a bolded title, subtitle, and axis labels."
#| fig-align: "center"
penguins |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = bill_length_mm,
                       y = bill_depth_mm,
                       color = species)) +
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~island, scales = "free")+
  labs(title = "Bill Geometry of Palmer Archipelago Penguins", # sets the title
       subtitle = "On the Islands of Biscoe, Dream, and Torgersen", # subtitle
       x = "Bill Length (mm)",  # X axis label
       y = "Bill Depth (mm)",   # Y axis label
       color = "Species")+      # labels the legend
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))   # makes the plot title bold
```

Great! We can clearly see in @fig-basic3 the beak geometry patterns across the *islands* and *species*.

---

### Changing the theme

What if you'd like to change the style of the plot to something a little more interesting?

Click "**Show code**" below to see how you can do this.

```{r}
#| label: fig-basic4
#| fig-cap: "Changing the point shape, size, opacity, and color scheme."
#| fig-align: "center"
penguins |> 
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = bill_length_mm,
                       y = bill_depth_mm,
                       color = species)) +
  geom_point(shape = 18, size = 3, alpha = 0.7)+   # Change the points
  facet_wrap(~island, scales = "free")+
  labs(title = "Bill Geometry of Palmer Archipelago Penguins",
       subtitle = "On the Islands of Biscoe, Dream, and Torgersen",
       x = "Bill Length (mm)",
       y = "Bill Depth (mm)",
       color = "Species")+
  theme_minimal()+                  # theme_minimal() sets the overall theme
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#a31621",
                                "#fed766",    # give it a nice color scheme
                                "#f77f00"))+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

```

With that, we have our **final plot**! All that is left to do is export it.
